blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but remain computationally expensive. Sparse attention and temporal caching reduce computation within and across denoising steps, respectively, offering a natural composition. However, predictions produced with sparse attention become sources for temporal reuse, coupling their errors along the sampling trajectory. We observe that improving the accuracy of these sources recovers fidelity without changing the reuse schedule, and that sparsification errors remain directionally aligned across nearby steps, suggesting that correction information can be shared rather than recomputed. These observations motivate RECAP, a training-free method that couples sparse attention with hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction, adaptively coordinated by online error feedback. Cached dense refinement corrects omitted interactions in current sparse estimates, while fresh sparse statistics track input changes and regulate the aging correction. The resulting predictions then renew the sources for whole-step prediction reuse, allowing prediction history to advance between dense refreshes. We evaluate RECAP on multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention methods, caching methods, and their direct compositions. On HunyuanVideo at 720p 5-second generation, RECAP achieves a 3.05x speedup and outperforms all tested direct compositions in both fidelity and inference speed.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Diffusion transformers have emerged as a powerful architecture for visual
generation ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) , but the quadratic complexity of
attention and repeated transformer evaluations make inference expensive.
Video generation is especially costly due to the length of its
spatiotemporal token sequences ( Yang et al., 2025b ; Kong et al., 2024 ) . Sparse attention reduces
the interactions computed within each denoising step ( Xi et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) , while temporal caching reuses features
or predictions across steps ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . Since the two
approaches save computation along different axes, a natural way to
accelerate further is to compose them directly. In such a composition,
however, sparse-attention predictions become the sources that caching
reuses in later steps. Sparsification error therefore affects both the
current sampler update and subsequent reused predictions, making the
accuracy of these sources central to the speed–fidelity trade-off.

We study this coupling in direct compositions and make two observations.
First, source accuracy matters for fidelity. When we replace the cached
tensors with dense counterparts while keeping the reuse schedule and the
sparse predictions used by the sampler, the deviation from the dense

suggests that a single dense correction can serve several sparse
evaluations, whose corrected predictions then provide more accurate
sources for temporal reuse. Sparse attention and caching should therefore
correct each other rather than act independently, as
Fig. 2 illustrates. Section 3.1 details both analyses.

Motivated by these observations, we propose Recap , which connects
sparse attention and a two-level cache hierarchy through reciprocal
correction, as illustrated in Fig. 3 . At the attention level, a
cached dense refinement supplies the detail that the current sparse
estimate leaves unresolved. As attention inputs evolve across steps,
fresh sparse statistics in turn regulate how strongly this aging
refinement is applied, so that cached and current information correct
each other. At the prediction level, the corrected outputs renew a
prediction cache, from which later steps are extrapolated without another
transformer evaluation. Sparse computation thus links the two levels,
and one dense refresh can support several sparse evaluations together
with the prediction reuse that follows them.

blocks.en: This design also naturally supplies the feedback for adaptive online scheduling. Each computed prediction reveals the error of the extrapolation it replaces, and each dense refresh reveals the error of the refinement it renews. Since corrected sparse evaluations renew prediction history while reusing existing refinement, the two caches can be renewed at different rates. The prediction error thus decides when to compute a new prediction, and the refinement error decides whether this computation needs a dense refresh. Under a fixed budget, these decisions choose among prediction reuse, corrected sparse computation, and dense refresh, adapting the schedule to each sample without offline search.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Sparse attention. Sparse attention exploits spatial and temporal patterns ( Xi et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Li et al., 2025 ) , or selects important
interactions through content-dependent scores ( Xia et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) ,
token reordering ( Yang et al., 2025a ; Hu et al., 2026 ) , and query–key
clustering ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . Training-based approaches further
learn sparse patterns ( Zhang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Instead of
discarding omitted interactions, PISA approximates them with block means
and shared first-order value compensation ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and COBS
estimates block mass with second-order key statistics ( Tian et al., 2026 ) .
Building on these approximations, Recap corrects the remaining tail
value and normalization mass with dense refinement cached from earlier steps.

blocks.en:
The two levels of reuse in Recap naturally supply the feedback
needed to schedule them. Each computed prediction reveals the error of
the extrapolation it replaces, and each dense refresh reveals the error
of the refinement it renews. Recap uses these errors to decide online
when to compute a new prediction and whether this computation needs a
dense refresh. The schedule therefore adapts to each sample as sampling
proceeds, rather than relying on offline search or a fixed reuse pattern.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We presented Recap , a training-free method that couples sparse
attention and hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction instead of composing them directly. We
showed that the accuracy of cache sources affects the fidelity of the
composition and that sparsification errors persist across nearby steps.
Building on these findings, Recap maintains a two-level cache
hierarchy. At the attention level, cached dense refinement corrects sparse
attention, while fresh sparse statistics regulate how strongly this aging
refinement is applied. At the prediction level, corrected predictions
renew the sources for whole-step reuse. Online error feedback
decides when to compute and when to refresh densely, so the schedule
adapts to each sample without costly offline search. Across three video
diffusion models, Recap improves the speed–fidelity trade-off over
individual accelerators and direct compositions, reaching a 3.05 × 3.05\times speedup on HunyuanVideo with higher fidelity than all tested compositions.
